title: Advanced Linux Administration
subtitle: 25 questions covering commands, networking, file systems, scripting, and system administration. Based on the ALA Post Test. Faster correct answers score more.

questions.q: Which command displays the first 10 lines of server_log.txt?
questions.note: head server_log.txt displays the first 10 lines of a file by default, making it ideal for quickly scanning the top of large log files without loading the whole file.

explain.correct: head prints the first 10 lines of a file by default.
wrong: cat prints the entire file, not just the first 10 lines.
tail shows the LAST 10 lines, the opposite of what's asked.
more pages through the whole file interactively rather than showing just the top.

questions.q: Which command changes a file's owner to 'john' and group to 'staff'?
questions.note: chown john:staff /path/to/file sets both the user owner (john) and the group owner (staff) in a single command. chmod changes permissions, not ownership.

explain.correct: chown sets a file's owner, and with the user:group form it sets the group too.
wrong: chmod changes permission bits, not ownership.
chgrp changes only the group, and 'john' is a user, not a group.
setfacl adds an ACL entry; it doesn't change the file's owner or group.

questions.q: Which command copies an entire directory recursively to another local location?
questions.note: cp -r copies a directory and all its contents recursively. mv moves (does not copy). rsync is better for incremental network syncs. ln -s creates a symlink, not a copy.

explain.correct: cp -r copies a directory and its contents recursively to a new local location.
wrong: mv MOVES (renames) the directory instead of copying it.
rsync -r can copy recursively, but it's a sync/transfer tool; cp -r is the direct local recursive copy the question asks for.
ln -s creates a symbolic link, not a real copy.

questions.q: Which command creates a new directory named project_docs in /home/user/?
questions.note: mkdir creates a new directory. touch creates an empty file. cp copies an existing path. rm -r deletes a directory and its contents.

explain.correct: mkdir creates a new directory at the given path.
wrong: touch creates an empty FILE or updates timestamps, not a directory.
cp copies existing items and this form is malformed; it won't create a directory.
rm -r DELETES recursively, the opposite of creating.

questions.q: Which command creates an empty file named config.txt in /home/user/?
questions.note: touch creates an empty file without writing any content. The echo redirect writes an empty string. mkdir creates a directory. cp copies an existing file.

explain.correct: touch creates an empty file (or updates its timestamp if it exists).
wrong: echo "" > file writes a newline, leaving a 1-byte file rather than a truly empty one.
mkdir makes a directory, not a file.
cp copies an existing file and is malformed here.

questions.q: The booting option ____ boots the system installed on the hard disk.
questions.note: 'Boot from Hard Disk' loads the operating system already installed on the disk. The other options launch the installation process in various modes.

explain.correct: 'Boot from Hard Disk' boots the operating system already installed on the disk.
wrong: 'Installation' launches the OS installer, not the installed system.
'Installation - ACPI Disabled' is an installer variant with ACPI off, still the installer.
'Installation - Safe Settings' is an installer variant with conservative options, still the installer.

questions.q: Which command enables a network device (eth0)?
questions.note: 'ip link set eth0 up' brings the interface up. 'down' disables it. 'enable' and 'start' are not valid ip link verbs.

explain.correct: ip link set eth0 up activates (brings up) the interface.
wrong: 'down' disables the interface, the opposite.
'enable' is not a valid ip link state; the keyword is up.
'start' is not a valid ip link state; the keyword is up.

questions.q: Ping keeps sending packets until terminated by pressing ______.
questions.note: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the foreground process, terminating ping and displaying the summary statistics. Ctrl-D signals end-of-input, not process termination.

explain.correct: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, which terminates ping.
wrong: Ctrl-A moves the cursor to the start of the line in the shell; it doesn't stop ping.
Ctrl-B moves back a character (or is a multiplexer prefix); it doesn't interrupt.
Ctrl-D sends end-of-file, not an interrupt signal.

questions.q: ping ____ specifies a timeout in seconds before ping exits regardless of packets sent.
questions.note: -w maxwait sets a deadline in seconds after which ping exits. -f is flood mode. -l preload sends that many packets without waiting. -n uses numeric output only.

explain.correct: ping -w sets a deadline in seconds after which ping exits regardless of packets sent.
wrong: -f is flood ping (send packets as fast as they return).
-l preload sends that many packets quickly at the start.
-n shows numeric output (skips DNS); it isn't a timeout.

questions.q: To define a mail server for a domain, which DNS record type is required?
questions.note: An MX (Mail Exchanger) record maps a domain to its mail server. SOA defines zone authority. NS lists name servers. CNAME is an alias record.

explain.correct: An MX (Mail eXchanger) record designates the mail server(s) for a domain.
wrong: SOA holds zone administration and serial data, not mail routing.
NS lists the authoritative name servers, not the mail server.
CNAME is an alias to another name and cannot serve as the domain's mail designation.

questions.q: The ____ bit prevents users from deleting each other's files in shared directories.
questions.note: The sticky bit on a directory means only the file owner, the directory owner, or root can delete a file. /tmp uses it. SUID runs the file as its owner; SGID as its group.

explain.correct: The sticky bit on a shared directory (e.g., /tmp) lets only a file's owner delete it.
wrong: SUID runs an executable as its owner; it isn't about deletion in shared directories.
SGID runs as the group or inherits the group on new files; not deletion protection.
SSID is a wireless network name, unrelated to file permissions.

questions.q: A(n) ____ ACL comprises entries for owner, owning group, and other -- matching conventional permission bits.
questions.note: A minimum ACL mirrors the three standard Unix permission entries (owner, owning group, other). An extended ACL adds named-user and named-group entries beyond those three.

explain.correct: A minimum ACL contains just the owner, owning-group, and other entries, matching the standard permission bits.
wrong: 'maximum' is not standard ACL terminology.
An extended ACL ADDS named-user/named-group entries beyond the basic three, the opposite of minimum.
'comprehensive' is not standard ACL terminology.

questions.q: The ____ format is a container for files and directories; archive files conventionally end in .tar.
questions.note: tar (Tape Archive) is the standard container format on Unix/Linux systems. .gz is a compression format. zip is a different archive format. exe is a Windows executable.

explain.correct: tar is the container format that bundles files and directories; archives end in .tar.
wrong: exe is a Windows executable, not an archive container.
zip is a compressed archive, but the conventional .tar container is tar.
gz (gzip) compresses a single stream and isn't itself a multi-file container.

questions.q: In Bash, which command performs arithmetic operations?
questions.note: The let command evaluates arithmetic expressions in Bash (e.g., let x=5+3). test evaluates conditions. cut extracts fields. cat concatenates files.

explain.correct: Bash's let evaluates arithmetic expressions.
wrong: cut extracts columns or fields from text.
test evaluates conditional (true/false) expressions, not arithmetic results.
cat concatenates and prints files.

questions.q: Every Makefile consists of targets, ____, and commands for the targets.
questions.note: A Makefile rule has the form: target: dependencies followed by commands. Dependencies list what must be built before the target. The three library types are unrelated to Makefile structure.

explain.correct: A Makefile rule consists of a target, its dependencies (prerequisites), and the commands to build it.
wrong: Static libraries are build inputs/outputs, not a structural part of a Makefile rule.
Shared libraries are build inputs/outputs, not a structural part of a Makefile rule.
Dynamic libraries are build inputs/outputs, not a structural part of a Makefile rule.

questions.q: The ____ program analyzes network connections to specific hosts.
questions.note: Traffic-vis is a network traffic visualization and analysis tool that examines connections to specific hosts. NFS is a file-sharing protocol; DNS resolves names; Proxy intermediates requests.

explain.correct: Traffic-vis analyzes and visualizes network connections to specific hosts.
wrong: NFS is a network file system, not a traffic analyzer.
DNS is the name-resolution service, not a connection analyzer.
A proxy is an intermediary for requests, not a connection-analysis tool.

questions.q: Which command removes the apache2 service from the init process?
questions.note: chkconfig apache2 off disables a service at init runlevels so it does not start automatically. top, vmstat, and iostat are monitoring tools -- they have no service management function.

explain.correct: chkconfig <service> off removes the service from the boot runlevels so it won't start at boot.
wrong: top is a live process monitor, not a service manager.
vmstat reports virtual-memory statistics.
iostat reports I/O statistics; it doesn't manage services.

questions.q: Which command stops a running instance of apache2?
questions.note: rcapache2 stop is the SUSE-style init script that stops the apache2 daemon. chkconfig manages runlevel enablement, not the running state. sysctl tunes kernel parameters. vmstat monitors I/O.

explain.correct: On SUSE-style systems the rc<service> script controls a running service; rcapache2 stop halts it.
wrong: chkconfig enables/disables a service at boot; it has no 'stop' action for a running instance.
sysctl tunes kernel parameters, not services.
vmstat reports memory statistics, not service control.

questions.q: Every swap partition has an entry in the file ____.
questions.note: /etc/fstab (filesystem table) lists all partitions and mount points, including swap partitions. The other paths do not exist as standard Linux files.

explain.correct: Swap partitions are listed in /etc/fstab, the filesystem table read at boot.
wrong: /etc/swap is not a real configuration file.
/swap/partitions is not a real configuration file.
/etc/sys/swap is not a real configuration file.

questions.q: The space on the ____ partition is used to free physical memory by copying temporarily unused pages.
questions.note: Swap space acts as virtual memory overflow -- the kernel pages out inactive memory to swap when RAM is under pressure, freeing physical memory for active processes.

explain.correct: The swap partition frees physical RAM by paging temporarily unused memory pages to disk.
wrong: 'listen' is not a type of partition used for paging.
'kernel' is not a partition used for paging.
'core' is not a partition used for paging.

questions.q: ___ displays system load averages for the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes.
questions.note: uptime shows how long the system has been running and the load averages for 1, 5, and 15-minute intervals. The other commands list files, tune kernel params, or are not standard commands.

explain.correct: uptime reports the system load averages for the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes (and time since boot).
wrong: ls lists directory contents.
sysctl reads/sets kernel parameters, not load averages.
chkcfg is not a standard command (and chkconfig manages services, not load).

questions.q: A comment is introduced with a(n) ____ character in shell scripts.
questions.note: Lines beginning with # are comments in bash and most Unix shells. The exception is the shebang (#!) on line 1. ! is history expansion; * is a glob; / is a path separator.

explain.correct: In shell scripts, # begins a comment; the rest of the line is ignored.
wrong: ! appears in the #! shebang or history expansion; alone it isn't a comment marker.
* is a glob wildcard, not a comment marker.
/ is a path separator or division operator, not a comment marker.

questions.q: The command ____ copies complete directories across a network to a different computer.
questions.note: rsync (remote sync) is designed for copying files and directory trees across a network efficiently using delta transfers. tar archives locally; mt manages tape devices; dd does raw block copies.

explain.correct: rsync efficiently copies whole directory trees across a network to another host.
wrong: tar archives files; it isn't the network directory-copy command here.
mt controls magnetic tape drives.
dd performs low-level block copies, not network directory sync.

questions.q: Name resolution is configured in the file ____.
questions.note: /etc/resolv.conf specifies the DNS nameservers and search domains used by the system resolver. The other paths are not standard Linux locations for this file.

explain.correct: Name resolution (the DNS resolver) is configured in /etc/resolv.conf.
wrong: /var/resolv.conf is the wrong path; the file lives in /etc.
/network/resolv.conf is the wrong path; the file lives in /etc.
/sys/resolv.conf is the wrong path; the file lives in /etc.

questions.q: The command _____ changes the ACL of a file.
questions.note: setfacl modifies (sets) Access Control List entries on a file or directory. getfacl reads/displays the current ACL. lsfacl and chgfacl are not real commands.

explain.correct: setfacl sets or modifies a file's Access Control List.
wrong: getfacl READS (displays) the ACL; it doesn't change it.
lsfacl is not a real command.
chgfacl is not a real command.
